Haley Stevens 'guilty of the very sin' behind 'misguided' MAGA endorsement: analysis
articles.description: Rep. Haley Stevens' (D-MI) endorsement of MAGA Senate candidate Mike Rogers not only injected new uncertainties into the Michigan Senate race, but also revealed a troubling pattern of behavior, according to a new analysis. Stevens rocked the Democratic Party on Sunday when she endorsed Rogers, a move that led multiple staffers to resign from her office and sparked bitter outrage among some political analysts. But her reasoning seemed to betray the message she was trying to deliver, according to Jonathan Chait, a staff writer for The Atlantic. "Stevens’ dramatic reversal met with immediate cries of opportunism or political stupidity," Chait noted. "But Stevens seems instead to be following through on a principled objection to [Abdul] El-Sayed’s rhetoric and associations that threaten the state’s Jewish population. The trouble is that her application of those principles is misguided, undermining the values she claims to uphold. Before this weekend, Stevens could credibly accuse El-Sayed of overlooking the bigotry of his allies out of political expedience. Now she, too, is guilty of that very sin." Haidt added that whatever message Stevens had hoped to send by endorsing Rogers has fallen on deaf ears. "Perhaps she is expressing a less-than-exalted notion, Nobody puts Haley Stevens in a corner, lashing out in humiliated defiance of El-Sayed for marginalizing her in the campaign’s final days. Or, even worse, she is communicating that prejudice against Jews is unacceptable but prejudice against Muslims and Arabs is not," he wrote.

articles.title: Are the US midterms going to see a blue wave of Democrats winning seats – or a blue flood?
articles.description: Donald Trump uttered five words this summer that could seal the Republican party’s fate: ‘Pretend I’m on the ticket’ He spoke admiringly of a senator’s posterior. He baselessly accused a Muslim candidate of being a terrorist. He boasted about his renovations of the White House. He quipped that his own supporters couldn’t afford a hamburger at his Mar-a-Lago club. Every now and then, he spoke about the cost of living, and other everyday concerns of voters. Donald Trump has held dozens of campaign rallies before next week’s US midterm elections. The 80-year-old remains convinced that he can prove the doubters wrong again and help Republicans retain control of the US Congress. But it was five words he uttered at this summer’s Republican convention in Dallas that could seal his party’s fate: “Pretend I’m on the ticket.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Piles of rubbish, power cuts and potholes: anger grows over Johannesburg’s run-down infrastructure
articles.description: The problems run deep in South Africa’s largest city. Will voters punish the ANC in next week’s local elections? One week before the local elections in South Africa, the pavements and roads of the Johannesburg township Alexandra were filled with piles of rubbish, rotting in the heat. At the Jukskei River, its banks choked with rubble and litter, foul-smelling brown water flowed out of a culvert. “We’ve got way too many challenges,” said Semadi Manganye, the chief executive of Alexandra Water Warriors, an environmental NGO that organises clean-ups of the river and plants trees on its banks. “If it’s not electricity, it’s water. If it’s not water, it’s waste.” Continue reading...
